questions.title: Effects of vagus nerve stimulation on thoracic and abdominal viscera
questions.question: Stimulation of the vagus nerve produces which combination of effects?

options.A: Slowed atrial rate, bronchial constriction and increased gut motility
options.B: Accelerated atrial rate, bronchial dilation and decreased gut motility
options.C: No effect on the heart, bronchial dilation only
options.D: Slowed atrial rate but decreased gut motility

explanations.A: Correct. The vagus nerve carries essentially the whole parasympathetic supply of the thoracic and abdominal viscera. Its stimulation slows the heart by acting on the atria (via the SA and AV nodes), constricts the bronchi, and drives gut motility and secretion forward - the coordinated "rest and digest" pattern of parasympathetic action on these organs. This combination of a slowed heart, constricted airways and an actively moving gut is the signature vagal effect tested repeatedly across this exam's autonomic questions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes roughly the opposite, sympathetic-type pattern (tachycardia, bronchodilation, reduced gut motility), not the parasympathetic vagal effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The vagus does affect the heart (slowing it) and does not dilate the bronchi; it constricts them.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The heart-slowing half is right, but the vagus increases, not decreases, gut motility - the opposite of what this option states.

questions.learning_objective: State the vagus nerve's parasympathetic effects on the heart, bronchi and gut: slowing the atria, constricting bronchi and driving gut motility.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-102 EOM - End foundation 2030.pdf p6 (same bank cited as EOM - end foundation مصريين 222 1.pdf p5), keyed (b).

questions.title: Autonomic fibre type serving sweat glands
questions.question: A student under exam stress notices dry mouth and a racing heart, both cholinergic-receptor effects at their respective effector organs. Which of the following is the one sympathetic postganglionic fibre type that is also cholinergic, unlike the rest of the sympathetic postganglionic outflow?

options.C: Fibres to the blood vessels of skeletal muscle

explanations.A: Correct. Autonomic fibres are named for the transmitter they release, and cholinergic fibres are every preganglionic fibre (sympathetic or parasympathetic) plus every postganglionic parasympathetic fibre. The sympathetic division's postganglionic fibres are otherwise adrenergic (releasing noradrenaline) - except for the postganglionic sympathetic fibres to sweat glands, which are the one recognised cholinergic exception in the sympathetic outflow. This is why a sympathetically driven stress response can still produce a cholinergic-type effect (sweating) alongside adrenergic ones (tachycardia).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Postganglionic sympathetic fibres to the heart are adrenergic, releasing noradrenaline to accelerate heart rate; they are not the cholinergic exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Postganglionic sympathetic fibres to skeletal muscle blood vessels are adrenergic in most textbook accounts of this level; they are not the named cholinergic exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The adrenal medulla is functionally a modified sympathetic ganglion innervated directly by preganglionic (cholinergic) fibres, but it is not itself a postganglionic fibre and is not the sweat-gland exception being tested here.

questions.learning_objective: State that postganglionic sympathetic fibres to sweat glands are cholinergic, the one exception to the otherwise adrenergic sympathetic postganglionic outflow.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-102 EOM - End foundation 2030.pdf p6, keyed (c), exam-stress vignette (dry mouth, tachycardia, cholinergic receptor type at sweat/salivary glands).

questions.title: Types of autonomic ganglion
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four recognised types of autonomic ganglion?

explanations.A: Incorrect as the answer to "NOT one of the four" - the paravertebral sympathetic chain ganglion is one of the four recognised autonomic ganglion types.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the answer - the terminal ganglion, where preganglionic parasympathetic fibres typically relay (often within or near the target organ), is one of the four recognised types.
explanations.C: Correct. There are four types of autonomic ganglion: the paravertebral sympathetic chain, the collateral (prevertebral) ganglia, the terminal ganglia, and the adrenal medulla (a modified sympathetic ganglion). The dorsal root ganglion, by contrast, holds the cell bodies of somatic sensory (not autonomic motor) neurons and is not one of the four autonomic ganglion types - it is part of the sensory, not the autonomic efferent, pathway.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the answer - the collateral (prevertebral) ganglion is one of the four recognised autonomic ganglion types.

questions.learning_objective: Name the four types of autonomic ganglion (paravertebral chain, collateral, terminal, adrenal medulla), and distinguish them from the sensory dorsal root ganglion.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-102 EOM - Final foundation 2030.pdf p15 (same bank cited as EOM - Foundation Final Egyptian.pdf p15), keyed (d, function of the autonomic ganglia).

questions.title: Relay site of preganglionic parasympathetic fibres
questions.question: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres typically relay in which type of ganglion?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The paravertebral sympathetic chain ganglion is where preganglionic sympathetic, not parasympathetic, fibres commonly relay.
explanations.B: Correct. Of the four autonomic ganglion types - paravertebral sympathetic chain, collateral, terminal, and adrenal medulla - the terminal ganglion is where preganglionic parasympathetic fibres relay onto their postganglionic neuron. Terminal ganglia sit within or very close to the wall of the target organ itself, which is why parasympathetic postganglionic fibres are characteristically very short compared with the long preganglionic parasympathetic fibre that reaches them. This short postganglionic length is a direct consequence of the terminal ganglion's location right next to (or inside) the effector organ.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Collateral (prevertebral) ganglia, such as the coeliac and mesenteric ganglia, relay preganglionic sympathetic fibres supplying abdominal viscera, not parasympathetic fibres.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The dorsal root ganglion holds somatic sensory neuron cell bodies; it plays no role in relaying autonomic motor (parasympathetic or sympathetic) fibres.

questions.learning_objective: State that preganglionic parasympathetic fibres relay in the terminal ganglion, located within or near the target organ, giving parasympathetic postganglionic fibres their characteristic short length.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-102 EOM - Final foundation 2030.pdf p15 (same bank cited as EOM - Foundation Final Egyptian.pdf p15), keyed (b, where preganglionic parasympathetic fibres usually relay).

questions.title: Preferred adrenergic subtype for treating bronchial asthma
questions.question: Which adrenoceptor subtype is the preferred pharmacological target for relieving bronchospasm in bronchial asthma?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Alpha-1 receptors mediate smooth muscle contraction (e.g. vasoconstriction, and internal urethral sphincter contraction); stimulating them would not relax bronchial smooth muscle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Alpha-2 receptors act chiefly as presynaptic autoreceptors inhibiting further noradrenaline release; they are not the target for bronchodilation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Beta-1 receptors are concentrated in the heart, where their stimulation increases rate and force of contraction; selectively targeting them would not be the preferred route to bronchodilation and risks unwanted cardiac stimulation.
explanations.D: Correct. Adrenergic receptors sit both on the effector organ and on the nerve ending that released the transmitter, and are classified into two alpha and three beta subtypes, distinguished by which second messenger system they engage. Beta-2 receptors are the subtype that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, which is why beta-2-selective agonists (such as salbutamol) are the preferred bronchodilator treatment for bronchial asthma, avoiding the cardiac stimulation that a non-selective beta agonist (acting on cardiac beta-1 receptors too) would cause.

questions.learning_objective: State that beta-2 adrenoceptors are the preferred pharmacological target for bronchodilation in asthma, distinct from cardiac beta-1 and vascular alpha receptors.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-102 EOM - Final foundation 2030.pdf p19 (same bank cited as EOM - Foundation Final Egyptian.pdf p19), keyed (d, better treatment for bronchial asthma).

questions.title: Effect of a sympathomimetic drug on bladder function
questions.question: A sympathomimetic drug is most likely to cause which of the following adverse effects, related to its adrenoceptor action?

explanations.A: Correct. Adrenergic receptors are split into alpha and beta subtypes sitting on their respective effector organs. At the bladder neck and internal urethral sphincter, alpha-1 receptor stimulation causes smooth muscle contraction, which opposes voiding; a sympathomimetic drug stimulating these receptors can therefore precipitate or worsen urinary retention, a recognised adverse effect particularly relevant in patients (such as older men) whose bladder outflow is already partly obstructed. This is the same adrenoceptor-subtype logic that, at a different effector organ (the bronchial tree), instead produces the beta-2-mediated bronchodilation exploited therapeutically in asthma.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increased salivation is a cholinergic (parasympathetic), not adrenergic, effect; a sympathomimetic drug would tend to reduce, not increase, salivary flow.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adrenergic stimulation (beta-2) causes bronchodilation, not bronchoconstriction; this option describes roughly the opposite effect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adrenergic (particularly beta-1) stimulation increases, not decreases, heart rate; a sympathomimetic would tend to cause tachycardia, not bradycardia.

questions.learning_objective: State that alpha-1 adrenoceptor stimulation at the bladder neck/internal urethral sphincter can cause urinary retention, a recognised adverse effect of sympathomimetic drugs.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-102 EOM - End foundation 2030.pdf p6 (same bank cited as EOM - end foundation مصريين 222 1.pdf p6), keyed (a, sympathomimetic drug - associated effect, urine retention).

questions.title: Cell body location of a preganglionic autonomic neuron
questions.question: Which statement is true of a preganglionic autonomic neuron, whether sympathetic or parasympathetic?

options.A: Its cell body lies within the target organ
options.B: Its cell body lies in the CNS (brainstem or spinal cord)

explanations.A: Incorrect. A cell body within the target organ describes the postganglionic parasympathetic neuron (relaying in a terminal ganglion at or in the organ), not the preganglionic neuron.
explanations.B: Correct. Every preganglionic autonomic neuron - sympathetic or parasympathetic - has its cell body within the central nervous system, in the brainstem or spinal cord, with its axon then leaving the CNS to synapse on a postganglionic neuron in a peripheral autonomic ganglion. This CNS origin is a defining, universal feature of the preganglionic neuron regardless of division, distinguishing it from the postganglionic neuron, whose own cell body sits in the peripheral ganglion itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Every preganglionic autonomic fibre, sympathetic or parasympathetic, is cholinergic (releasing acetylcholine) at its ganglionic synapse, not adrenergic; adrenergic transmission belongs to most postganglionic sympathetic fibres instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Preganglionic autonomic fibres are typically myelinated (B fibres), not unmyelinated, which is part of why they conduct relatively quickly to reach their ganglion.

questions.learning_objective: State that every preganglionic autonomic neuron, sympathetic or parasympathetic, has its cell body in the CNS and is cholinergic at its ganglionic synapse.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-102 EOM - Final foundation 2030.pdf p21 (same bank cited as EOM - Foundation Final Egyptian.pdf p21), keyed (b, true statement about preganglionic nerves).

questions.title: Classification of the Na+-K+ pump as a transport mechanism
questions.question: The Na+-K+ ATPase pump, which moves three sodium ions out of the cell for every two potassium ions moved in, is classified as:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Facilitated diffusion moves a substance down its concentration gradient via a carrier protein without using ATP directly; the Na+-K+ pump moves both ions against their gradients and consumes ATP directly, which facilitated diffusion does not.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Secondary active transport uses the electrochemical gradient built by a primary active transporter (such as the Na+-K+ pump itself) to move a different solute, often via a cotransporter; it does not directly hydrolyse ATP the way the pump itself does.
explanations.C: Correct. The Na+-K+ pump is ATP-driven primary active transport, directly hydrolysing ATP to move three sodium ions out of the cell for every two potassium ions moved in, against both ions' concentration gradients. Because it moves unequal charge (3 positive charges out for 2 in), the pump is also electrogenic, contributing directly to the resting membrane potential in addition to maintaining the ionic gradients themselves. This direct ATP-hydrolysis, against-the-gradient, electrogenic transport is what defines it as primary, not secondary or facilitated, active transport.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Simple diffusion is passive, unassisted movement down a concentration gradient with no protein and no energy expenditure; the Na+-K+ pump is the opposite - active, protein-mediated, and moving both ions against their gradients.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Na+-K+ pump is ATP-driven primary active transport, electrogenic because it moves three sodium out for every two potassium in.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-102 EOM - Final foundation 2030.pdf p14 (same bank cited as EOM - Foundation Final Egyptian.pdf p14), keyed (c).

questions.title: Why an anticholinesterase relieves myasthenia gravis
questions.question: Myasthenia gravis is caused by autoantibodies directed against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction. Why does an anticholinesterase drug relieve its muscle weakness?

options.C: It prolongs acetylcholine's action at the remaining receptors by slowing its breakdown
options.D: It replaces acetylcholine with a longer-acting analogue

explanations.A: Incorrect. An anticholinesterase does not repair or regenerate receptors that autoantibodies have destroyed or blocked; the receptor loss itself is not reversed by this drug class.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Anticholinesterases do not act on the autoantibodies at all; they act purely on the enzyme that normally breaks down acetylcholine, leaving the autoimmune process itself untouched.
explanations.C: Correct. Myasthenia gravis is caused by autoantibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, reducing the number of functional receptors available at the neuromuscular junction and so weakening neuromuscular transmission. An anticholinesterase drug inhibits acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that normally breaks down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, which prolongs acetylcholine's presence and action there. With more time to act on the fewer remaining receptors, this compensates - functionally, not by fixing the underlying autoimmune receptor loss - for the reduced receptor number, which is exactly why an anticholinesterase relieves the disease's muscle weakness.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Anticholinesterases do not supply any acetylcholine analogue; they act only by slowing the breakdown of the acetylcholine already being released.

questions.learning_objective: Explain why an anticholinesterase relieves myasthenia gravis: by prolonging acetylcholine's action on the reduced number of remaining nicotinic receptors, not by reversing the underlying antibody-mediated receptor loss.
